lead: A diode rectifier turns AC into pulsating DC using only the one-way conduction of a diode. The average output is fixed by the supply peak and the circuit shape; no gate signal can change it. Half-wave, centre-tap full-wave and bridge circuits are the three standard shapes. They appear in low-cost chargers, soldering irons, DC motor field supplies and as the front end of many power supplies before a filter. This chapter derives their average and RMS output, ripple, peak inverse voltage and diode count.
prereq: You need: the diode V-I characteristic and static resistance from Unit 1, especially that a conducting diode drops about 0.7 V and a reverse-biased one blocks until its peak inverse voltage.

sections.h3: Half-wave rectifier with R and RL load

blocks.text: One diode connects the AC source to the load. During the positive half-cycle the diode conducts and the load sees v = Vm sin θ. During the negative half-cycle the diode blocks and the load voltage is zero. The output is a train of positive half-sine pulses, one per supply cycle.
Vdc = (1/π) ∫₀^π Vm sinθ dθ = Vm/π = 0.318 Vm
blocks.where: Vdc is the average output voltage in V; Vm is the peak supply voltage in V.

blocks.text: Vrms = √((1/π) ∫₀^π Vm² sin²θ dθ) = Vm/2 = 0.5 Vm
blocks.where: Vrms is the RMS output voltage in V; θ is the angle in radians.
RF is the ripple factor, dimensionless. PIV is the largest reverse voltage across the diode, PIV = Vm. Output ripple is at the supply frequency f: 50 Hz supply gives 50 Hz ripple.

blocks.text: With a purely resistive load the current copies the voltage and falls to zero at θ = π. With an RL load and no freewheeling diode, the inductor keeps the diode on after π; the output voltage follows the supply negative until the current decays. A freewheeling diode across the load gives the inductor current a path at θ = π, so the output voltage clips at zero and the load current stays positive. That clipped waveform has a higher average than the raw RL case. Transformer utilisation factor TUF = Pdc / transformer VA rating is poor, about 0.287, because the transformer carries DC magnetising current and is idle for half the cycle.

A centre-tapped transformer and two diodes make a full-wave rectifier. The secondary has two equal halves, each giving Vm peak with respect to the centre tap. On the positive half-cycle diode D1 conducts; on the negative half-cycle D2 conducts. Each diode sends current through the load in the same direction, so the output has two pulses per supply cycle.

blocks.where: Vdc is the average output voltage in V; Vm is the peak of each half-secondary in V.

blocks.text: Vrms = √((1/π) ∫₀^π Vm² sin²θ dθ) = Vm/√2 = 0.707 Vm
blocks.where: Vrms is the RMS output voltage in V.

FF is the form factor; RF is the ripple factor. PIV of each diode is 2Vm: when D1 conducts, D2 is reverse-biased by the full secondary voltage, that is 2Vm measured from one end of the secondary to the other. Output ripple is at 2f.

blocks.text: Some syllabi call this a two-pulse rectifier and write p = 2, where p is the number of output pulses per supply cycle. TUF is about 0.693. The circuit needs a special centre-tapped transformer, and each diode must withstand twice the peak that a bridge diode sees for the same output.

Four diodes in a bridge give full-wave output without a centre tap. D1 and D3 conduct on one half-cycle; D2 and D4 conduct on the other. The load current direction is the same in both halves. The AC supply connects to two opposite nodes of the bridge (the junctions of D1-D2 and D3-D4), and the load connects across the other two opposite nodes, which become the DC positive and DC negative terminals.
Vdc = 2Vm/π;   Vrms = Vm/√2;   PIV = Vm;   RF = 0.482;   TUF ≈ 0.812
blocks.where: Vm is the peak supply voltage in V; PIV is the reverse voltage per diode in V. PIV of each bridge diode is Vm. When D1 and D3 conduct, D2 and D4 are each reverse-biased directly across the supply (through a conducting diode), so each blocks the full Vm on its own. The bridge PIV is Vm because each diode sits across the supply, not because the diodes share voltage.

blocks.text: A few syllabi call this a full-wave bridge to separate it from the centre-tap type. The bridge is the common choice: no centre tap, smaller transformer, better TUF, but two diode drops in the conduction path, about 1.4 V for silicon. A half-wave circuit uses one diode and has RF 1.21; a full-wave circuit uses two or four diodes and has RF 0.482. Firing-angle control replaces these diodes with thyristors in 2.3.

examples.question: A single-phase bridge rectifier feeds a 100 Ω resistive load from a 230 V rms, 50 Hz supply. The diodes are ideal. Find the peak supply voltage Vm, average output voltage Vdc, average load current Idc, RMS output voltage Vrms, RMS load current Irms, ripple factor, peak inverse voltage PIV of each diode and output ripple frequency.
steps: RF = √((Vrms/Vdc)² − 1) = √((230.0/207.07)² − 1) = 0.483. The rounded form factor 1.11 gives the usual 0.482.
examples.answer: The bridge gives Vm = 325.27 V, Vdc = 207.07 V, Idc = 2.07 A, Vrms = 230.0 V, Irms = 2.30 A, ripple factor 0.483, PIV 325.27 V and 100 Hz output ripple.
examples.check:
import math
Vm = 230*math.sqrt(2)
Vdc = 2*Vm/math.pi
Idc = Vdc/100
Vrms = Vm/math.sqrt(2)
Irms = Vrms/100
RF = math.sqrt((Vrms/Vdc)**2 - 1)
PIV = Vm
print(round(Vm, 2))
print(round(Vdc, 2))
print(round(Idc, 2))
print(round(Vrms, 2))
print(round(Irms, 2))
print(round(RF, 3))
print(round(PIV, 2))
print(100)

traps: Quoting the full-wave ripple factor 0.482 for a half-wave circuit, whose ripple factor is 1.21.
Giving the centre-tap PIV as Vm instead of 2Vm.
Using 230 V as Vm. For a 230 V rms supply, Vm = 230√2 = 325.3 V.
Saying the bridge output ripple is at f. Full-wave output ripple is at 2f.
Mixing the average formulas: half-wave Vdc = Vm/π, full-wave Vdc = 2Vm/π. TUF is not efficiency.

quiz.q: What is the PIV of each diode in a bridge rectifier with peak supply Vm?
A full-wave rectifier runs from a 50 Hz supply. What is the output ripple frequency?
Why is the PIV of a centre-tap rectifier diode 2Vm?
quiz.a: When one diode conducts, the other is connected across the whole secondary, so it blocks the peak voltage of the whole secondary, 2Vm.

quiz.q: A half-wave rectifier uses a 230 V rms, 50 Hz supply and R = 50 Ω. Find Vm, Vdc, Idc and PIV.
A bridge and a centre-tap rectifier give the same Vdc from the same peak Vm. Compare diode count, PIV per diode and transformer.
quiz.a: Bridge: 4 diodes, PIV = Vm, no centre tap, TUF about 0.812. Centre-tap: 2 diodes, PIV = 2Vm, needs a centre-tapped transformer, TUF about 0.693. The bridge is preferred for high voltage.

quiz.q: A bridge rectifier has Vm = 100 V and R = 20 Ω. Find Vdc and Irms.
What does a freewheeling diode do in a half-wave rectifier with RL load?
quiz.a: It takes over the inductor current when the supply voltage falls to zero, clips the output voltage at zero and keeps the load current positive. Without it the output voltage goes negative after π and the average output falls.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real bridge modules are rated by average forward current and surge current, and datasheets give VF versus current. Diode drop matters at low output voltages: a 1.4 V bridge drop is 7% of a 20 V rail but negligible at 300 V. Thermal design uses the conduction loss P = 2 VF IF(av) for a bridge, plus reverse recovery loss at high frequency. Search 'bridge rectifier datasheet', 'PIV derating' and 'inrush current' next.
